articles.body: Originally published at nlocoding.com 94% of software testing teams now use AI—yet only 12% have achieved full autonomy in their AI integration, according to BrowserStack in 2026.[1] AI tools for collaborative software testing are now the rule, not the exception AI has become nearly universal in software testing, with 94% of teams integrating AI into their processes in 2026.[1] But integration doesn’t mean mastery: only 12% of those teams have achieved full autonomy, leaving most constrained by fragmented workflows. articles.title: Amazon Interview Question: Your LRU Cache Works. Now Make It Expire.
articles.excerpt: walkthrough of expiration, stale timers, and the small detail that can delete the wrong value. You have the hash map. You have the linked list. Your LRU cache passes the example, and you are mentally…
articles.body: walkthrough of expiration, stale timers, and the small detail that can delete the wrong value. You have the hash map. You have the linked list. Your LRU cache passes the example, and you are mentally packing up your interview nerves. Then the follow-up arrives: every entry needs an expiration time, and you cannot keep scanning the entire cache to find what has expired. Lovely. Our tidy little data structure has acquired a calendar. I like this question because you can understand the first bug with two entries and five seconds. No giant architecture diagram required. Once we fix that bug, a second one appears when somebody updates a key before its old timer fires. This TTL-aware LRU cache question from a reported Amazon interview. The prompt is freely readable.

articles.title: 12 pagination test cases every API client should pass
articles.excerpt: Most pagination bugs I've seen weren't in the happy path. Page 1 works, page 2 works, and then someone asks for page 0, or the last page has exactly limit items, or a cursor gets cut off in a URL, and…
articles.body: Most pagination bugs I've seen weren't in the happy path. Page 1 works, page 2 works, and then someone asks for page 0, or the last page has exactly limit items, or a cursor gets cut off in a URL, and the client either loops forever or quietly drops data. I build testingapis.com , a free fake API for testing clients, and while adding pagination endpoints to it I wrote down every edge case I could think of. Here's the list. The requests point at my API so you can see a real response, but the point is to run the same cases against your own API.

articles.title: Building an evidence-based job application tracker with Rails 8, pgvector and Claude
articles.excerpt: A typical job ad lists ten or more requirements. When I apply, the hard part isn't can I prove this? So I built Evidex, a job application tracker that checks every requirement in an evidex.henockmulli…
articles.body: A typical job ad lists ten or more requirements. When I apply, the hard part isn't the cover letter; it's answering honestly, for each requirement, can I prove this? And if I can, where is the evidence: which project, which line of my CV? So I built Evidex , a job application tracker that checks every requirement in an ad against your own CV and project documents, and cites the passages that support each verdict. It's live with a public demo (no sign-up): evidex.henockmullissa.dev , and the code is on GitHub . This post walks through how it works: the stack, the retrieval pipeline, how one structured Claude call judges every requirement, and the part I'd keep in any LLM project: checking the model's answer on the server before trusting it.

Gemini may soon allow you to select multiple conversations at once, for easy bulk deletion. At this point, it’s probably fair to say that a growing number of us have a bit of a love–hate relationship when it comes to many things AI. Sure, we appreciate its ability to help summarize reams of material, generate fantastical imagery, and even help us code apps , but all that power is also exactly why it’s worth approaching with a modicum of caution. articles.body: Astronomers have spotted a remarkable gamma-ray burst (GRB) that's a real Incredible Hulk compared to other cosmic explosions of the same type. What makes this GRB so special is the fact that the central engine powering it remained active for around 27 days, flaring in X-rays following the initial blast. That's 20 days longer than the longest previous GRB on record. This record-breaking burst — which is designated GRB 220706A and was spotted on July 6, 2022 — is even more exciting because scientists don't know what the central engine powering it actually is. "In a nutshell, GRB 220706A is an extremely late X-ray flare.
